title: Can a Lemon Light a Bulb?
paragraphs: Can a lemon make electricity?
It sounds like magic, but it is a real science experiment.
You can try it at home with a grown-up.
All you need is a lemon, two kinds of metal, some wires, and a tiny light.
First, read each instruction carefully before you start.
Roll the lemon on a table to make it extra juicy inside.
Next, push a nail coated with zinc into one side of the lemon.
Then push a strip of copper into the other side.
The two metals must be different, or nothing will happen.
Inside the lemon, the sour juice is full of acid.
The acid slowly eats away at the zinc.
As this happens, the zinc lets go of tiny bits called electrons.
The electrons want to travel over to the copper.
When you connect the two metals with a wire, the electrons rush through it.
That flow of electrons is electricity!
Sadly, one lemon makes only about 0.9 volts.
That is not enough to light a tiny bulb called an LED.
So people connect three or four lemons in a row.
Each extra lemon adds a little more electricity.
Together, the lemons can make the LED glow softly.
Oranges and even potatoes can work too.
If you remove one nail, the path breaks and the light goes out.
Here is a surprise: the power really comes from the zinc, not from the lemon!

factNotes: A lemon battery uses two different metals (zinc anode, copper cathode) with acidic juice as the electrolyte; current comes from oxidation of zinc -> https://chem.libretexts.org/Courses/University_of_California_Davis/UCDemos/Orange_Lemon_Battery

Galvanized (zinc-coated) nail can replace the zinc strip; citric acid reacts with zinc, electrons flow through the wire to copper -> https://www.scienceworld.ca/resource/lemon-battery/

Single copper/zinc lemon cell about 0.9 V; at least two cells in series needed to power an LED; 'The energy does not come from the lemon or potato' (it comes from zinc); potatoes work too -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemon_battery

Four lemons with copper and galvanized nails light an LED; scienceworld suggests groups of 3 or 4 lemons in series -> https://www.sciencing.com/light-led-lemon-5824362 ; https://www.scienceworld.ca/resource/lemon-battery/
Oranges also work as fruit batteries -> https://chem.libretexts.org/Courses/University_of_California_Davis/UCDemos/Orange_Lemon_Battery
Rolling the lemon to make it juicier is a common kit instruction (procedural tip, not a scientific claim)
summary: A lemon can make a little electricity. You push a zinc nail and a copper strip into it. The sour acid eats the zinc, and tiny electrons move through a wire to the copper. One lemon is too weak to light an LED, so people join three or four lemons together.

title: Why Do Chameleons Change Color?
paragraphs: Many people think chameleons change color only to hide.
That is just one small part of the story.
There are more than 200 kinds of these lizards, and many live on the island of Madagascar.
Scientists have found that their shifting colors are mostly a way to send messages.
A chameleon's skin has a unique trick.
Inside its skin cells are tiny crystals, much too small to see.
When the chameleon is calm, the crystals sit close together, and its skin looks green.
When it gets excited, the crystals spread apart.
Then its skin can flash bright yellow, orange, or red.
These colors show how a chameleon feels.
When two males meet, they often turn bright colors to warn each other.
A male may also show off his brightest colors to attract a female.
A chameleon that is scared or angry often turns dark.
Color also helps a chameleon stay warm or cool.
On a cold morning, it turns darker to soak up more heat from the sun.
When it gets too hot, it turns lighter.
Chameleons cannot match every color around them, but they have other ways to stay safe from a predator.
Their eyes can move in different directions at once.
One eye can gaze at a hungry bird while the other eye looks for bugs.
Some kinds even sway back and forth, like a leaf in the wind.

factNotes: More than 200 chameleon species; many (76) found only on Madagascar; eyes move in different directions so one can watch a threat while the other scans; darken in cold to absorb heat and lighten while basking; turn dark when stressed, scared, or angry; cannot change to match any color; color change usually for signaling (attract mates, show aggression) -> https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/reptiles/facts/chameleons

Color change works by changing the spacing of nanocrystals in iridophore skin cells: relaxed = close together (blue reflected, which mixes with yellow pigment to look green); excited = spread apart (yellow, orange, red); males change dramatically when facing a rival male or trying to attract a female -> https://www.livescience.com/50096-chameleons-color-change.html
Mood/communication and temperature are main drivers; camouflage usually not the main motivation -> https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/how-do-chameleons-change-colour/
Dark colors absorb heat, light colors reflect heat -> https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/explainer-how-do-chameleons-change-colour/uqarhcepe
Some chameleons rock back and forward to look like leaves blown by the wind -> https://www.howitworksdaily.com/?p=1213
summary: Chameleons do not change color only to hide. Tiny crystals in their skin move closer or farther apart to make new colors. The colors show feelings, like being calm, angry, or showing off. Colors also help them warm up or cool down, and their moving eyes help them stay safe.

title: Yao Ming, the Gentle Giant
paragraphs: Yao Ming was born in Shanghai, China, in 1980.
His mother and father were both basketball players, and they were very tall.
Even as a baby, Yao was big.
He weighed about 5 kilograms at birth, more than twice as much as most newborn babies in China.
He started playing basketball when he was nine years old.
Yao kept growing until he was 229 centimeters tall.
He played for the Shanghai Sharks in China for five years.
Then, in 2002, the Houston Rockets picked him first in the NBA draft.
His NBA career had a slow start.
In his very first game, he scored zero points!
But he soon became an outstanding center and was chosen as an All-Star eight times.
Fans in China were enthusiastic about Yao.
Millions of them woke up early to watch his games from America.
In 2007, Yao played against Yi Jianlian, another player from China.
More than 200 million people in China watched that one game.
The leader of the NBA called Yao a bridge between fans in China and fans in America.
He also carried China's flag at two Olympic Games.
Sadly, Yao hurt his feet and ankle again and again.
In 2011, he stopped playing.
In 2016, he joined the Basketball Hall of Fame, and the Rockets retired his number 11 shirt the next year.
Later, he became the chief of China's basketball group.
Yao showed how one player can bring the whole international basketball world closer together.

title: Gyeongju: The Golden City of Silla
paragraphs: Gyeongju is a city in the southeast of Korea.
Long ago, it was the capital of an ancient kingdom called Silla.
Silla lasted from 57 BC to AD 935, which is almost 1,000 years.
For that whole time, Gyeongju was its capital city.
Old Silla treasures are found all over the city.
In the middle of Gyeongju, you can see giant grassy hills that are really royal tombs.
A park called Daereungwon has 23 of these tombs.
Kings, queens, and nobles were buried inside them long ago.
In 1973, workers dug into one tomb called Cheonmachong.
They found more than 11,000 treasures inside.
One was a shining gold crown, and another was a painting of a flying white horse.
The people of Silla also studied the sky.
Nearby stands Cheomseongdae, a stone tower about 9 meters tall.
It was built in the 600s, when Queen Seondeok ruled.
People may have used it to watch and record the stars.
It is the oldest observatory still standing in East Asia.
On a mountain east of the city, Silla built Bulguksa Temple and a stone cave called Seokguram.
Inside the cave, a large stone Buddha sits quietly.
In 1995, both became UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
For hundreds of years, Korea was split into three kingdoms.
Silla, Goguryeo, and Baekje often fought one another.
Then Silla teamed up with China's Tang dynasty.
Together, they defeated Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.
After that, much of Korea was united under Silla.
Today, visitors walk among the tombs and imagine Silla's golden days.

title: The Clock That Saved Basketball
paragraphs: On November 22, 1950, two NBA teams played one of the strangest games ever.
The Fort Wayne Pistons beat the Minneapolis Lakers by a score of 19 to 18.
It is still the lowest-scoring game in NBA history.
How could two pro teams score so few points?
Back then, there was no limit on how long a team could keep the ball.
The Lakers had a giant star named George Mikan, and he was very hard to stop.
So the Pistons coach told his players to just hold the ball.
They passed it back and forth, and almost nobody tried to shoot.
The fans booed and stomped their feet in anger.
Many people began to think pro basketball was boring.
Danny Biasone owned a team called the Syracuse Nationals.
He was desperate to make games exciting again.
He figured that a good game had about 120 shots in all.
A game lasted 48 minutes, which is 2,880 seconds.
He divided 2,880 by 120 and got the number 24.
So he said a team must shoot within 24 seconds of getting the ball.
The NBA started using the 24-second clock in the 1954-55 season.
Now players had to move swiftly, and teams could not stall anymore.
That season, teams scored more than 13 extra points per game.
Games became much faster and more fun to watch.
Many people conclude that this simple clock saved the NBA.
Today, it is still an essential part of every game.

title: Who Really Built the Pyramids?
paragraphs: The Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt is a magnificent monument.
It was built about 4,500 years ago for a king named Khufu.
When it was new, it stood 146 meters tall.
For centuries, many people believed that slaves built it.
But scientists have found clues that tell a different story.
In 1990, a tourist was riding a horse near the pyramids.
The horse stumbled over a low wall hidden in the sand.
The wall turned out to be part of a tomb.
Soon, experts found the graves of many pyramid workers.
The workers were buried close to their king's pyramid, which was a great honor.
In some tombs, there were jars that once held bread and beer.
Experts say slaves would never have been buried this way.
These builders were paid workers, and they ate well.
Every day, farms sent about 21 cattle and 23 sheep to feed them.
About 10,000 people worked on a pyramid at one time.
Many of them worked for three months and then went back home.
How did they move stones that were as heavy as a big car?
Workers set each load on a wooden sled and used ropes to drag it across the sand.
An old Egyptian wall painting shows a man pouring water in front of a sled.
In 2014, scientists tested this idea in a lab.
They found that the right amount of water cut the pulling force in half.
Dry sand piles up in front of a sled, but damp sand stays firm.

title: Jun's Extra Pass
paragraphs: Jun was the fastest player on the Tigers.
Every time he got the ball, he dribbled down the court by himself.
He took almost every shot, even when three defenders surrounded him.
His teammates stood with their hands up, waiting for passes that never came.
After one loss, Jun and his friend Max had a quarrel in the locker room.
Max shouted, "You never pass!"
That night, Jun watched a pro game on TV with his grandfather.
The players passed the ball five times before anyone took a shot.
Grandpa said, "Great players make their teammates better."
Slowly, Jun began to grasp what Max had been trying to tell him.
One player cannot beat five defenders alone.
The next Saturday, the Tigers played the Hawks for the championship.
With ten seconds left, the score was tied at 30.
Jun raced down the court, and two Hawks jumped in front of him.
Then he saw Max standing all alone near the basket.
Jun bounced the ball between the two defenders, right into Max's hands.
Max made an easy layup just before the buzzer.
The Tigers won 32 to 30, and the excited crowd cheered.
Max ran over and gave Jun a big high five.
"Best pass of the year," he said with an enthusiastic grin.
Jun had scored only four points, but he felt prouder than ever.
That one pass was his greatest accomplishment of the season.
From then on, Jun was a supportive teammate who looked for the open player.

title: The Secret Codes of Fireflies
paragraphs: On warm summer evenings, tiny lights blink on and off above the grass.
These lights come from fireflies, which are also called lightning bugs.
Fireflies are not really flies at all.
They are beetles, and there are about 2,000 kinds of them.
After nightfall, they use their lights to talk to each other.
A firefly makes its light in its belly.
Oxygen mixes with a special chemical called luciferin, and the belly begins to glow.
A light bulb gets hot, but a firefly's light makes almost no heat.
That is why people call it cold light.
Each kind of firefly has its own flash signal, like a secret code.
Males fly through the air and flash their pattern to attract a mate.
Many females wait on the ground or in plants and watch.
In one common kind, the male makes a one-second flash about every five seconds.
If a female likes what she sees, she waits about two seconds and flashes back.
The male follows her answers until he finds her.
Some fireflies use these codes to play an astonishing trick.
Females in one group, called Photuris, copy the flashes of other kinds of fireflies.
When a male of that kind flies down to meet her, she grabs him and eats him.
She even uses chemicals from his body to protect herself.
For such a tiny creature, the firefly has a clever and sometimes sneaky way to talk.

title: Iceland: Land of Fire and Ice
paragraphs: Iceland is an island country in the North Atlantic Ocean.
It sits high up in the Northern Hemisphere, just south of the Arctic Circle.
Fewer than 400,000 people live there.
People often call it the land of fire and ice, and it is easy to see why.
Huge sheets of ice called glaciers cover about one tenth of the land.
Iceland also has around 30 active volcano systems.
Some of these volcanoes are hidden under a glacier!
When hot lava melts the thick ice, the water can rush out in big floods.
In 2010, a volcano named Eyjafjallajokull blew a huge cloud of ash into the sky.
Planes all over Europe had to wait.
The heat under the ground warms water, too.
About 90 percent of homes in Iceland are heated with this hot water.
The country has more than 120 swimming pools, and nearly all of them are heated the same way.
Icelanders swim in outdoor pools all year, even in winter.
Every child must learn to swim at a young age.
Iceland's high latitude also gives it very strange days.
In June, the sun in the capital city sets just before midnight and rises again before 3 in the morning.
The sky never gets fully dark.
In December, there are only about 4 or 5 hours of daylight.
The arctic fox is the only native land mammal in Iceland.
Long ago, it walked there across the frozen sea.

title: Tiny Chips, Giant Jobs
paragraphs: Look inside almost any phone, car, or game console, and you will find chips.
A chip is a thin, flat piece of silicon, a material that comes from ordinary sand.
Many chips are only about the size of your fingernail.
Yet they work as the tiny brains and memories of our machines.
Each chip holds billions of tiny switches called transistors.
A transistor can be turned on or off, just like a light switch.
On can stand for 1, and off can stand for 0.
By flipping switches very fast, a chip can show a picture, play a song, or connect you to a video call.
For example, the main chip in the iPhone 15 Pro holds about 19 billion transistors.
Chips come in different types with different jobs.
Processor chips work like a brain, because they do math and follow instructions.
Memory chips work like a notebook, because they hold information until it is needed.
Building either kind is extremely hard.
So chips are made in special factories called fabs.
Inside a fab, the air is kept even cleaner than the air in a hospital.
Workers wear white "bunny suits" to protect the chips.
Even one speck of dust can ruin them!
Some of the most important chipmakers in the world are in Asia.
In Korea, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are the two biggest makers of DRAM, a common memory chip.
In Taiwan, a company called TSMC builds chips that other companies design.
Apple and Nvidia, for instance, design many of their own chips but have TSMC produce them.
Without these little pieces of silicon, most machines around us could not work.

title: From Lonely Boy to Great Khan
paragraphs: More than 850 years ago, a boy named Temujin was born on the wide grasslands of Mongolia.
When he was only eight years old, his father was poisoned by enemies from another tribe.
Soon afterward, most of his father's people left.
His family was left almost alone.
To survive, they gathered roots and nuts, caught fish, and hunted small animals.
Those hard years taught Temujin to be tough, patient, and clever.
At that time, the Mongols were split into many tribes that often fought one another.
As Temujin grew up, he made friends with some leaders.
He battled against others.
Step by step, he managed to unite most of the tribes under his command.
In 1206, a great meeting of Mongol leaders gave him a new title, Genghis Khan.
Historians still argue about what the name means.
One common idea is "universal ruler."
Genghis Khan and the Mongol armies that came after him built a gigantic empire.
Their skilled riders could cross huge distances quickly on strong, sturdy horses.
At its largest, the empire stretched from the Pacific Ocean all the way to central Europe.
It became the largest connected land empire in history.
To rule such an enormous area, the Mongols needed a fast way to send a message.
So they set up the yam, a chain of relay stations.
The stations were usually 20 to 40 miles apart.
At each station, a messenger could grab some food and a fresh horse, then race on.
In this way, important news could travel 120 miles or more in a single day.
The same safe roads also helped merchants trade silk and other goods along the Silk Road.

title: The Netherlands: A Country That Fights the Sea
paragraphs: Imagine living in a home that sits lower than the sea right next to it.
For many people in the Netherlands, that is simply normal life.
In fact, the name Netherlands literally means low lands or low countries.
About 26 percent of the land lies below sea level.
Around 60 percent of the country is at risk of flooding.
For hundreds of years, the Dutch have fought back against the water.
They built dikes, which are long, strong walls of earth that hold back the sea and rivers.
Around the 1200s, they also began using windmills to pump water out of low, wet areas.
Land that is dried out this way and kept dry is called a polder.
At a village called Kinderdijk, 19 windmills built around 1740 still line the narrow canals.
Today, electric pumping stations there do the hard work instead.
Even so, the sea sometimes wins.
During the night of January 31, 1953, a powerful storm pushed seawater over and through the dikes.
By morning, huge areas were underwater, and more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands had died.
After this disaster, the Dutch decided that stronger protection was essential.
They began a giant project called the Delta Works, a system of dams and storm barriers.
One barrier opened in 1986 and is almost 9 kilometers long.
Its giant metal gates can close when a dangerous storm comes.
The last major piece, a barrier near the city of Rotterdam, was finished in 1998.
Today, the country has about 17,500 kilometers of dikes and sand dunes.
Thanks to all this work, experts call the Netherlands one of the safest river deltas in the world.

title: The Honest Call
paragraphs: With twenty seconds left in the championship game, Min's team, the Hawks, led by one point.
The gym was so loud that Min could barely hear his own breathing.
A Tiger player dribbled toward the basket, and Min jumped to block him.
The ball bounced off Min's fingertips and rolled out of bounds.
The referee had been watching another player, so he had to guess.
"Hawks' ball!" he shouted, pointing at Min's team.
Min's teammates cheered, and his friend Daniel slapped him on the back.
"We've got this game now," Daniel whispered.
Min's legs began to tremble, but not because he was exhausted.
He knew the ball had touched him last, so the Tigers deserved to keep it.
Nobody else seemed to know, and staying quiet would almost guarantee a victory.
Still, Min pictured holding the trophy with a secret inside, and his stomach twisted.
Before he could change his mind, Min walked over to the referee.
"It touched me last," he mumbled, staring at his shoes.
"What did you say?" the referee asked.
Min took a deep breath and said it again, louder.
The referee nodded and gave possession to the Tigers.
The Hawks groaned, and Daniel looked desperate as the clock started again.
Seconds later, the Tigers scored, and the final buzzer sounded.
The Hawks lost by one point, and Min felt a sharp sting of disappointment.
But in the handshake line, the Tigers' captain stopped in front of him.
"That was the bravest play of the whole game," the captain said.
On the bus, Coach Park told Min that people forget scores but remember honest players.
Min concluded that he did not regret his choice, because he was proud of how he had played.

title: Copper: The Metal Inside Our Wires
paragraphs: Look inside almost any electrical cord, and you will find thin threads of orange-brown metal.
That metal is copper, element number 29 on the periodic table.
Its chemical symbol is Cu, which comes from cuprum, an old Latin word for copper.
People have been shaping copper into useful tools for at least 8,000 years.
Copper fills our wires because it is excellent at letting electricity flow.
Metals like copper conduct electricity, which means they carry it from place to place.
Among all metals, only silver does this job better.
Silver costs much more, though, so copper is the smarter choice for most wires.
Copper also bends easily and can be stretched into long, thin wires without breaking.
These wires connect our lamps, chargers, and televisions to the power in the walls.
About three quarters of all copper produced goes into wires, cables, and electronics.
Copper has a famous job outside of wires, too.
The Statue of Liberty in New York has a skin made of thin copper sheets about as thick as two pennies.
An iron structure inside holds up the sheets, like a skeleton holds up your body.
When the statue was unveiled in 1886, it was a shiny reddish brown, like a brand-new penny.
So why is Lady Liberty green today?
Over many years, air and water slowly reacted with the copper on her surface.
This reaction formed a thin green coating called a patina.
The change took time, and the statue was half green by 1910 and completely green by about 1920.
Surprisingly, the green layer protects the copper underneath from wearing away.
Her color demonstrates that a metal can form a new layer that guards it.

title: The Clay Army of China's First Emperor
paragraphs: In March 1974, farmers in China were digging a well in their village.
Their shovels hit broken pieces of clay figures.
They had no idea how important their discovery would be.
Soon, archeologists rushed to the site, about 20 miles east of the city of Xi'an.
Underneath the fields lay an entire army made of terracotta, or baked clay.
So far, experts have counted more than 8,000 life-size soldiers.
There are also 130 chariots and about 670 horses.
Most of the soldiers are between 1.75 and 2 meters tall.
They are arranged in long rows, ready for battle.
Each one seems to have its own face, so no two look exactly alike.
The army also held real bronze weapons, such as spears and crossbows.
Why would anyone build an army out of clay?
Nearby is the huge tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a united China.
Many experts believe these fierce soldiers were made to guard him after his death.
Work on his tomb began in 246 BC, when he was just 13 years old.
About 700,000 workers labored on the project for nearly 30 years.
The excavation is still going on today, and it moves slowly on purpose.
When the soldiers were first made, they were painted to look real.
However, once they were uncovered, much of the paint flaked off within minutes in the dry air.
Because of this, archeologists now work extremely carefully so the remains do not crumble.
Many areas have not been dug up yet, so more soldiers may still be waiting underground.
In 1987, the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a treasure for the whole world.

title: Eight Planets and One Bright Star
paragraphs: Imagine a giant racetrack in space where eight planets circle one bright star, lap after lap.
That star is our Sun, and its family of planets, moons, and space rocks is called the solar system.
The Sun's gravity works like an invisible rope, holding every planet on its path.
The curved path that a planet follows around the Sun is called its orbit.
Starting closest to the Sun, the planets line up in this order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
The first four are small, rocky worlds with hard ground you could stand on.
The last four are giants made mostly of gas and ice, and they have no solid surface at all.
Our own planet, Earth, sits third in line, at a distance of about 93 million miles from the Sun.
Even so, sunlight crosses that enormous gap in just over eight minutes.
Jupiter, the fifth planet, is by far the biggest of them all.
If Earth were the size of a grape, Jupiter would be about as big as a basketball.
Its next-door neighbor, Saturn, is famous for its wide, shining rings.
From far away they look like solid hoops, but they are really made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.
Farther out, Uranus and Neptune are freezing ice giants, and Neptune needs about 165 Earth years to circle the Sun once.
For many years, students learned that there were nine planets, not eight.
The ninth was Pluto, a tiny, icy world that lies beyond Neptune.
In 2006, a group of scientists called the International Astronomical Union agreed on new rules for what counts as a planet, and Pluto did not pass.
They reclassified it as a dwarf planet instead.
Pluto itself did not change one bit, but the way scientists sort our solar system did.

title: Wilma Rudolph: From a Leg Brace to Gold
paragraphs: Wilma Rudolph was born early in Tennessee in 1940, and she was a tiny, fragile baby.
She was the 20th of 22 children in her big family.
As a young girl, she battled pneumonia, scarlet fever, and polio, which badly weakened her left leg.
Doctors said she would never walk again, and she had to wear a brace on her leg.
Her family refused to give up on her.
Every week for two years, Wilma made a 100-mile round trip to a hospital in Nashville for treatment.
At home, her family massaged her weak leg four times a day.
Her determined effort finally paid off, and by the time she turned 12, she could walk without a brace.
Before long, she was flying down the court for her high school basketball team.
Soon, Wilma began training with Ed Temple, the track coach at Tennessee State University.
In 1956, at only 16, she won a bronze medal in a relay race at the Olympics in Melbourne, Australia.
It was an outstanding accomplishment for a teenager, but Wilma had her heart set on something even bigger.
At the 1960 Olympics in Rome, she became the champion of the 100-meter dash, crossing the finish line in just 11.0 seconds.
Three days later, she won the 200-meter dash as well.
Finally, she ran the last leg of the 4x100-meter relay with her college teammates and helped them win gold too.
With that race, she became the first American woman to win three gold medals in track and field at a single Olympics.
In both 1960 and 1961, she was named the Associated Press Female Athlete of the Year.
The girl who was once told she would never walk had become one of the fastest women on the planet.

title: The 1992 Dream Team
paragraphs: For many years, NBA stars were not allowed to play at the Olympics.
That changed on April 7, 1989, when FIBA, the international group that runs basketball, voted 56 to 13 to let professional players compete.
Three years later, the "Dream Team" from the United States arrived at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona, Spain.
It had 11 NBA players, including Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson, and Larry Bird, plus one college star, Christian Laettner.
Eleven of those 12 players were later elected to the Basketball Hall of Fame on their own.
The Dream Team played some of the most magnificent basketball the world had ever seen.
It won all eight of its games by an average of 43.8 points.
The team made 58 percent of its shots.
In the gold medal game, it beat Croatia 117 to 85, and that 32-point win was its closest game of the tournament.
Coach Chuck Daly never called a single timeout during the entire Olympics.
Off the court, the players were treated like rock stars, and even their rivals were starstruck.
During one game, a player guarding Magic Johnson waved to a teammate on the bench to take a photo of them.
That kind of friendly interaction showed how much the world admired these players.
Around the globe, kids who watched the Dream Team started dreaming about the NBA.
One of them was Pau Gasol, a Barcelona boy who was not yet a teenager in 1992 and later won two NBA titles.
In France, young Tony Parker was inspired too, and he later wore number 9 because Michael Jordan had worn it in Barcelona.
When the 2024-25 NBA season began, its teams had 125 international players from 43 countries.
Today, players of almost every nationality share the same courts, and the Dream Team helped open the door.

title: Ant Cities: The Leafcutter Farmers
paragraphs: In the warm forests of South America, long lines of ants march along, each one holding a piece of green leaf over its head.
These are leafcutter ants, and one worker can carry a leaf piece 20 times heavier than its own body.
Yet the ants never eat a single bite of the leaves they work so hard to collect.
Instead, they are gathering food for something else: a fungus that grows inside their nest.
Back underground, the ants crush the leaf pieces into tiny pellets and press them into a spongy fungus garden.
The fungus feeds on the leaves, and the ants feed on the fungus, which is the only food leafcutter ants eat.
Scientists believe ants began farming like this about 50 million years ago.
In a way, these tiny insects were farmers millions of years before humans.
A leafcutter colony works like a busy city, and an ant's size helps decide its job.
The smallest workers, called minims, stay underground to care for the fungus, the eggs, and the young ants.
Medium-sized workers cut and carry leaves, and some minims ride on the leaves to fight off attacking flies.
The largest workers, called majors, guard the nest and keep the busy trails clear.
Other workers carry trash to separate rooms and stay away from the colony to keep it clean.
The colony has just one queen, who lays the eggs and can live for 15 to 20 years.
A colony can grow to as many as eight million workers.
Their nest can stretch 50 feet across and 16 feet deep.
That enormous nest gives the entire colony shelter from heat, rain, and hungry enemies.
No ant could survive alone, so every worker pulls its weight, and the chief goal of all of them is the colony's survival.

title: Why Volcanoes Erupt
paragraphs: Deep underground, rock can get so hot that it melts into a thick, glowing liquid called magma.
Magma can reach a temperature of 1,200 degrees Celsius, several times hotter than a kitchen oven.
Because magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it slowly pushes its way upward.
Sometimes it collects in a giant underground pocket called a magma chamber.
Magma also holds dissolved gases, a bit like the bubbles hidden in a closed bottle of soda.
While the magma stays deep down, the heavy rock above presses on it and keeps those gases trapped.
As the magma rises, that pressure drops, and the gases form bubbles, like soda when you open the cap.
When the bubbles grow quickly, they can make the magma surge upward and blast out all at once.
This theory also explains why fast-rising magma usually causes the most explosive eruptions.
Volcano scientists cannot see inside a mountain, so they search for evidence that magma is on the move.
Rising magma often cracks the rock around it and sets off swarms of small earthquakes.
It can also make the ground swell like a balloon, which scientists measure with GPS and tilt meters.
Gas detectors check whether more sulfur dioxide gas is leaking out each day.
In 1991, these warning signs saved thousands of lives at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines.
The volcano had been quiet for about 500 years, but in March, nearby villagers began to feel earthquakes.
By late May, the sulfur dioxide pouring out each day had jumped from about 500 tons to more than 5,000 tons.
Scientists warned that a huge eruption was coming, and in an emergency evacuation, at least 58,000 people left by June 12.
Three days later, Pinatubo produced the world's largest eruption in more than 50 years.
Its ash cloud shot up to 34 kilometers high, far above where airplanes fly.

title: Why Ice Floats
summary: Ice floats because water grows bigger when it freezes. Its tiny parts lock into a pattern with open spaces, so ice weighs less than the same amount of space filled with water. Most of an iceberg hides under the sea. In winter, floating ice covers lakes like a lid, and fish stay alive in the water below.
paragraphs: Here is an easy experiment you can try at home.
Follow these instructions carefully.
First, fill a glass with water.
Then remove an ice cube from the freezer and drop it in.
The ice does not sink to the bottom.
Instead, it bobs at the top, with most of the cube under the water.
Why does solid ice float in liquid water?
The answer is that water grows bigger when it freezes.
As water turns into ice, its tiny parts lock together in a neat pattern.
This pattern leaves small open spaces between them.
So the same water takes up about 9 percent more room as ice.
That is why a cube of ice weighs less than a cube of water of the same size.
Things that are lighter for their size float on things that are heavier.
You can see this on a giant scale with icebergs.
An iceberg is a huge chunk of ice that breaks off a glacier and falls into the sea.
About 90 percent of an iceberg hides below the water.
Only the small tip shows above the waves.
That is why ships must stay far away from icebergs.
Floating ice is also very important for fish.
In winter, a lake freezes from the top down.
The ice forms a lid over the lake.
Below the lid, the deep water stays at about 4 degrees Celsius.
Fish can keep swimming there all winter long.
If ice sank instead, a lake could freeze solid from the bottom up, and the fish would have nowhere to go.

title: Dribble Like a Pro
summary: Long ago, basketball players were not allowed to dribble. Today, dribbling is a key skill. Keep your eyes up, use both hands, and push the ball with your fingertips. Stay low when a defender is close, and practice every day without quitting.
paragraphs: When basketball was invented in 1891, players could not dribble at all.
They had to throw the ball from the spot where they caught it.
Today, dribbling is one of the most important skills in the game.
A good dribbler can move swiftly past defenders and help teammates score.
The good news is that anyone can get better with a few daily drills.
The first rule is to keep your eyes up.
If you stare at the ball, you cannot see open teammates or the basket.
Try this drill with a friend or a supportive parent.
While you dribble, your partner holds up some fingers.
You must call out the number without looking down.
The second rule is to use both hands.
If you dribble with only one hand, defenders will soon guess which way you will go.
Set up a few chairs and dribble around them.
Go once with your right hand and then once with your left.
Push the ball with your fingertips, not your flat palm.
The third rule is to stay low when a defender is close.
Bend your knees and keep the ball below your waist.
For a fun challenge, dribble while you kneel on the floor.
This drill makes your fingers and wrists stronger.
Practice for ten minutes every day, and do not quit when you lose the ball.
Dribbling also helps you stay in shape, because you keep moving the whole time.
Soon you may feel daring enough to try a crossover move in a real game!

title: Leo Finds His Shot
paragraphs: Leo loved basketball more than anything else.
He practiced his shots every day after school.
But at night, he liked to watch basketball videos on his tablet in bed.
Sometimes he stayed up until ten or even eleven o'clock.
One Saturday morning, Leo felt slow and sleepy at practice.
His legs felt heavy, and he yawned between drills.
He missed shot after shot, even the easy ones near the basket.
Leo dropped the ball and frowned.
"Why can't I make anything today?" he asked.
Coach Rivera sat down next to him on the bench.
"How late did you go to bed last night?" she asked.
Leo looked down at his shoes and said, "After eleven."
Coach Rivera nodded slowly.
"Sleep is when your body grows and repairs your muscles," she said.
"It also helps your brain remember the new moves you practiced.
Without enough rest, you have less energy for the game."
That night, Leo and his dad made a new evening routine.
Leo put his tablet away one hour before bed.
Then he brushed his teeth, read a short book, and turned off the light at eight thirty.
He went to bed at the same time every night.
At first, the new habit felt strange.
After two weeks, though, Leo felt wide awake at practice.
His shots were steady, and more of them swished through the net.
Leo smiled, because now he knew that a good night's sleep helps him play his best.

title: The First Olympic Games
paragraphs: Every four years, athletes from around the world meet at the Olympic Games.
But the Olympics did not begin in a big modern stadium.
They began in ancient Greece almost 2,800 years ago.
The first Games we have records of took place in 776 BC.
The Games were held at Olympia, a holy place for the Greek god Zeus.
One old legend says the hero Heracles planted the olive trees there.
At first, there was only one event, a running race called the stadion.
Each contestant sprinted one length of the track, about 192 meters.
Our word "stadium" comes from the name of this race.
The first champion we know about was a cook named Koroibos.
He did not get a gold medal or any prize money.
Instead, he was crowned with a wreath made of olive leaves.
The leaves came from a special olive tree that belonged to Zeus.
To the Greeks, this simple crown was a very great honor.
The Greek cities often fought wars with each other.
Before each Games, they announced a truce, which was a promise not to fight.
It let athletes and fans travel safely to Olympia.
Over the centuries, more events were added, such as wrestling, boxing, and chariot races.
The festival grew to five days and included a big ceremony for Zeus.
Today, the Olympic flame is still lit at Olympia before each Games.

title: Hang On and Get Stronger
short: The Pull-Up Bar and Your Muscles
paragraphs: A pull-up bar looks simple, but it is one of the most powerful tools for building strength.
All you do is grab the bar, hang, and pull your chin up over it.
That one move makes many muscles work together as a team.
Your back muscles do most of the pulling, while your arms and shoulders help.
Before you can pull, though, you have to hold on.
Your grip comes from muscles in your hands and forearms, the part of your arm between your wrist and elbow.
Hanging from a bar trains these muscles to squeeze hard and not let go.
Even your belly muscles join in, keeping your body balanced instead of swinging.
Here is a surprise: hard exercise actually makes tiny tears in your muscles.
These tears are far too small to see, and they are a normal part of getting stronger.
After you exercise, your body sends blood and nutrients to repair them.
Much of this repair work happens while you rest and sleep.
Foods with protein, such as eggs, fish, beans, and milk, give your body the material it needs.
Each time your muscles recover, they become a little stronger than before.
If you cannot do a pull-up yet, start with a dead hang.
Simply hold on to the bar with straight arms for as long as you safely can.
Try a few short hangs each day to build a steady habit.
Ask a grown-up to check that the bar is strong and safe.
If your hands or shoulders start to hurt, let go and rest.
With patient practice, one day you may pull your chin right over the bar!

title: Homes That Move: Life in a Mongolian Ger
paragraphs: On the wide grasslands of Mongolia, some families do not stay in one place.
They are herders who raise horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and camels.
These animals are often called the "five snouts" of Mongolia.
Because the animals eat the grass, herders must keep moving to find fresh pasture and water.
Many families move with the seasons, and they bring their whole house along!
Their home is a round tent called a ger, used by native Mongolians for centuries.
The walls are wooden lattice that folds up like a baby gate, and long poles hold up the roof.
Thick felt made from sheep's wool covers the frame and keeps out winter winds.
An experienced family can pitch a ger in one to three hours and take it down in about one.
The pieces are then packed flat and carried to the next camp.
Inside, a ger is cozy and carefully arranged.
A stove sits in the middle, and its smoke escapes through a round opening in the roof.
The door almost always faces south, toward the sunshine and away from the cold north wind.
Honored guests sit at the back of the ger, across from the door.
One ger can be a bedroom, kitchen, and living room for up to 15 people.
Mongolian herders are also famous for being hospitable.
The grasslands are huge, homes are far apart, and the weather can be harsh.
A traveler may need shelter, food, or a warm drink, so families help one another.
Guests are usually offered milk tea and dairy foods before anyone starts talking.
After all, the same herders might need a friendly door on their next long journey.

title: The Great Wall: Built Over Many Centuries
paragraphs: The Great Wall of China is not really just one wall.
It is a long chain of walls, towers, and forts across mountains, deserts, and grasslands.
In 2012, Chinese experts finished a five-year survey that measured all of its sections.
The total came to about 21,196 kilometers, more than half the distance around Earth!
No single builder could ever finish such a magnificent project.
The work began more than 2,500 years ago, when small kingdoms built walls along their borders.
Around 220 BC, Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, ordered many walls joined.
Over the following centuries, other rulers repaired old sections and added new ones.
Most of the wall seen today was rebuilt during the Ming dynasty, from 1368 to 1644.
Many older walls were packed earth, but Ming builders often used brick and stone.
The wall gave protection against raiders who attacked from the north.
Soldiers lived in watchtowers and forts and kept a lookout from high ground.
Each tower was like a small fortress, with space for supplies and firewood.
When guards spotted an enemy, they had to warn others quickly, long before telephones.
Their answer was a clever signal system that passed from tower to tower.
During the day, guards sent up columns of smoke, and at night they used fires.
Under Ming rules, the number of signals even showed how large the enemy army was.
One torch and one cannon shot meant that about 100 enemies were coming.
Five torches and five cannon shots meant that about 10,000 were on the way!
Tower by tower, the warning raced along the wall so the army could get ready.

title: The Countess Who Wrote for a Machine
paragraphs: Ada Lovelace was born on December 10, 1815.
Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron.
Her parents separated when she was only a baby, so she never got to know him.
Her mother did not want Ada to follow her father into poetry, so she pushed her toward mathematics and science instead.
Still, Ada never lost her imagination.
At age 12, she studied birds closely because she wanted to learn how to fly.
She wrote about her ideas in a book she called "Flyology."
In 1833, when she was about 17, Ada met an inventor and mathematician named Charles Babbage.
He invited her to see his Difference Engine, a calculating machine that he was still building.
Babbage later dreamed up an even more powerful machine, called the Analytical Engine, that could follow a list of instructions.
In 1843, Ada translated an article about the Analytical Engine that an Italian named Luigi Menabrea had written in French.
She added her own notes, and they ended up about three times longer than the article itself!
In one note, now called Note G, she carefully arranged the steps the machine would follow to work out a series of numbers called Bernoulli numbers.
Because of this, many people call Note G the first computer program and Ada the first computer programmer.
Some historians point out that Babbage had written simpler programs earlier, but he never published them.
Ada also imagined that such a machine might one day work with things besides numbers, such as musical notes.
Sadly, the Analytical Engine was never built.
As a result, no one could test her program while she was alive.
She died on November 27, 1852, when she was only 36 years old.
Much later, a computer language was named "Ada" in her honor.
Today, every computer that follows a program is evidence that her accomplishment was far ahead of its time.

title: Hoops on Wheels
paragraphs: In 1945, a new sport began rolling across the floors of two American hospitals.
Those hospitals cared for soldiers who had come home from World War II.
Many of the players had been badly injured in the war and now used wheelchairs, but they still wanted to compete.
Their game, wheelchair basketball, soon caught on.
By 1960, it was part of the Paralympic Games in Rome, with 96 athletes from 12 countries.
The court and backboards are the same as in regular basketball.
The hoop still hangs 3 meters, or 10 feet, above the floor.
Imagine sinking a shot from a sitting position, with no legs to help you jump!
A player may push the wheels only twice while holding the ball, and then the player must bounce it or pass it.
Pushing a third time without bouncing the ball is called traveling, just like taking too many steps in a regular game.
The chairs are an important aspect of the sport, because they are built for speed and quick turns.
Their two big wheels slant inward at the bottom.
One or two tiny wheels at the back keep the chair from tipping over.
Each player also gets a score from 1.0 to 4.5, and a higher score means the player's body can do more on the court.
The five players a team has on the court can add up to no more than 14 points at any time.
This rule makes sure that teams include players with many different abilities.
Games are fast and daring, and sometimes chairs crash and tip over, but players get back up and keep going.
Enthusiastic crowds cheer, and supportive teammates encourage each other after every miss.
The United States has been the most successful nation, with 10 men's and four women's Paralympic gold medals.
Those athletes prove that a wheelchair cannot stop anyone who refuses to quit.

title: The Forest With a Famous Nickname
paragraphs: The Amazon rainforest covers about 6.7 million square kilometers, an area roughly twice the size of India.
It stretches across eight countries and one territory, but nearly 60 percent of it lies in Brazil.
Winding through the forest is the Amazon River, which flows for more than 6,600 kilometers.
About 15 percent of all the river water pouring into the world's oceans comes from this one giant river.
The Amazon covers only about 1 percent of Earth's surface, yet it is home to at least 10 percent of all known species.
Pink river dolphins swim in its waters.
Green anacondas, the heaviest snakes on the planet, slide along its banks.
The entire forest holds an estimated 400 billion trees of roughly 16,000 different kinds.
Around 2.2 million Indigenous people live there too, and together they speak about 300 languages.
For years, people have called the Amazon "the lungs of the planet," and some have claimed it makes 20 percent of the oxygen we breathe.
Scientists say that number is far too high.
Trees do give off oxygen in the daytime, but they also use oxygen.
At night, they take in more oxygen than they give out.
Tiny living things that break down fallen leaves and dead wood use up much of the rest.
In the end, the forest's overall oxygen gift is close to zero.
Most of the oxygen in our air was actually made over billions of years by tiny ocean life called phytoplankton.
Does that mean the Amazon is not important?
Not at all.
It pulls huge amounts of carbon dioxide out of the air and helps keep rain falling across South America.
One scientist even said it works more like a giant air conditioner than a pair of lungs.
Since the survival of so many plants, animals, and people depends on this forest, its protection matters to the whole world.
